changes.main: "Look for the head, hairy thorax, banded abdomen, six legs, and two pairs of veined wings. The stated length measures the body; antennae extend beyond it."
"A reconstruction with a horizontal body, balancing tail, two walking legs, and two fingers on each small hand. Surface colors and soft tissues are illustrative."
"Follow the antennae back to the head. Insects have three main body regions: head, thorax, and abdomen. Turn the view to find the matching antenna on the other side."
"Look through the translucent wing and trace its supporting veins. The smaller hindwing sits behind the forewing. Both pairs attach to the thorax."
"Count three legs on this side, then orbit to find the other three. Each leg bends at joints; the hind legs in this illustration carry golden pollen loads."
"The red shell is a pair of hardened forewings called elytra. Follow the seam where they meet. The flight wings fold beneath these protective covers."
"These paired structures extend from the head. Compare their short, curved shape with the longer antennae on the honeybee."
"Look below the wing cases for three pairs of jointed legs. Six legs are one of the features that identify an insect."
"Move around the opening between the jaws to inspect the teeth. The soft tissues and colors are illustrated; the skeleton provides the evidence for the overall body plan."
"Trace the taper from the hips to the tip. The long tail extends behind a horizontal body, rather than resting on the ground."
"Follow the powerful hind leg down to its toes. T. rex supported its body on two hind legs; its small forelimbs did not serve as walking legs."
"These folds are called cristae. They pack more inner membrane into a small space. The membrane contains machinery involved in producing ATP, a molecule cells use to transfer energy."
"The outer membrane encloses the mitochondrion. Open the cutaway to compare this enclosing surface with the folded inner membrane beneath it."
"Look at the shallow depression in the disc. Orbit to see the matching indentation on the opposite face. This is a surface shape, not a hole through the cell."
"Compare the thicker rim with the thinner center. Normal red blood cells are flexible discs. Hemoglobin inside them carries oxygen around the body."
"Follow one continuous strand around the helix. Each backbone alternates sugar and phosphate groups. The second strand winds alongside it."
"The rungs represent pairs of bases between the two backbones. A pairs with T, and C pairs with G. The colors help distinguish parts of this conceptual model."
"Choose a numbered landmark to move closer. Orbit around the feature, then use Fit object to see the whole specimen."
"Use the ★ target button below the finder to locate it in the sky."
"View from Earth · north or south up"
"Drag to rotate · use + or − to zoom"
"Earth sits between the Sun and Moon. The large view below shows the Moon crossing Earth’s shadow."
"The Moon sits between the Sun and Earth. The large view below shows their apparent disks from an observer on Earth."
"Choose a solar or lunar eclipse, then follow the alignment from first overlap to maximum and back out. The stage buttons let you inspect each part at your own pace."
"The Moon appears large enough to cover the Sun’s bright disk completely. The corona appears in this model only when the whole disk is covered."
"The Moon appears smaller than the Sun. Even at maximum alignment, a bright ring remains visible. Solar viewing protection is required throughout."
"The Moon crosses off-center and covers only part of the Sun. The percentage above measures the covered area of the solar disk. Solar viewing protection is required."

"The penumbra gently dims the Moon. The umbra produces a much darker, often copper-colored region. Watch the shadow cross the disk: the sunlit part stays bright until it enters the shadow. Lunar eclipses are safe to view directly."

"This is an adjustable geometry demonstration, not a prediction of a dated eclipse. Sizes, distances, paths, timing, and shadow colors are illustrative. Coverage is calculated from the disks shown; it is not a measure of safe viewing or sky brightness. The Moon’s rim and Earth’s shadow boundaries are highlighted to make the geometry easier to follo
"Cool and faint, near the lower end of the main sequence."
"Near the part of the main sequence occupied by the Sun."
"Cool yet bright: a large radiating surface is needed."
"Very luminous. Temperature and luminosity alone do not establish a supergiant classification."
"Near the broad diagonal where stars fusing hydrogen in their cores are commonly found."
"Hot but faint: the inferred radiating surface is small, as in the white-dwarf region."
"Outside the highlighted teaching regions. A position alone does not identify a stellar type or life stage."
"Hertzsprung–Russell diagram: brighter stars are higher, hotter stars are left"
"Drag on the diagram, or focus it and use arrow keys. Left is hotter, up is brighter. Home returns to the Sun. Both axes use logarithmic spacing."
"Filled marker: your star. Gold dot: Sun. Purple rings: logged observations."
"Disk sizes are compressed so small and giant stars stay visible. Radius follows the Stefan–Boltzmann relation: luminosity depends on surface area and temperature."
"Shaded regions and example stars are teaching guides, not measured catalog points or an evolution track. Region boundaries are approximate. The Sun reference uses 5,772 K and one solar luminosity."
"Move a star across the diagram to see how temperature, luminosity, and radius relate. Compare examples, then log positions to keep them on the chart."

"The luminosity slider uses a log scale, so faint and bright stars are easy to reach. Mass is recorded separately and does not move the point or set its radius. These independent controls do not predict a star’s evolution."
"Radius is inferred from luminosity and effective temperature using a solar reference of 5,772 K. Star colors and region outlines are illustrative."

changes.before: "Design the structure to elastically resist seismic forces. Works for moderate quakes but becomes uneconomic for major ones — a strength-only bridge would need to be extraordinarily massive."
changes.main: "Provide enough strength for the intended seismic demands, with carefully detailed connections and supports. Strengthening one component can increase forces in adjacent components, so engineers check the complete load path."
changes.candidate: "Design the structure to elastically resist seismic forces. Works for moderate quakes but becomes uneconomic for major ones — a strength-only bridge would need to be extraordinarily massive."

changes.before: "Design specific elements to YIELD + DEFORM plastically during major quakes — absorbing energy without rupturing. Plastic hinges in columns are common. Steel works wonderfully here; brittle materials (cast iron, plain concrete) do NOT. The bridge sustains damage but doesn't collapse."
changes.main: "Detail selected regions, such as column plastic hinges, to yield through repeated cycles and dissipate energy. Other components are designed to resist the forces those regions can transmit. This can reduce collapse risk, but permanent damage may occur."
changes.candidate: "Design specific elements to YIELD + DEFORM plastically during major quakes — absorbing energy without rupturing. Plastic hinges in columns are common. Steel works wonderfully here; brittle materials (cast iron, plain concrete) do NOT. The bridge sustains damage but doesn't collapse."

changes.before: "Place the bridge superstructure on lead-rubber bearings or sliding bearings. The ground shakes; the bearings absorb most of the motion; the bridge above moves much less. Most aggressive new approach. Common in Japanese + Chilean + California bridges."
changes.main: "Flexible or sliding bearings allow relative movement between the deck and its supports, which can reduce transmitted acceleration and forces. The bearings need room to move; added energy dissipation helps limit that travel. Isolation can increase deck displacement even while reducing forces."
changes.candidate: "Place the bridge superstructure on lead-rubber bearings or sliding bearings. The ground shakes; the bearings absorb most of the motion; the bridge above moves much less. Most aggressive new approach. Common in Japanese + Chilean + California bridges."

changes.main: "Stand on the walkway at eye level. Drag to look around. With the view focused, ↑/↓ walk, ←/→ turn, Page Up/Down look vertically, and Home resets. The camera stays level as the deck moves."
"Deck view · Drag to look · ↑/↓ walk · Home reset"

"Energy balance: net input = kinetic + elastic + dissipated. Values are per kg of modal mass in the relative-motion model. Net input can fall when motion returns energy; cumulative dissipation does not decrease."
"Absolute ground and deck displacement over 24 seconds, measured from a fixed reference. The vertical marker follows experiment time; shaking ends at 16 seconds."
"actual model displacement; the 3D scene magnifies motion 10×."

"A truss, arch, or suspension bridge can have many vibration modes. These examples vary assumed stiffness per unit mass, not the bridge family. Compare peaks under the same input and damping, then choose a mode to inspect."

"Explore inertia with F = m × a. Choose an assumed mass and acceleration, then follow the unit conversion. Acceleration is a direct input here; it is not predicted from earthquake magnitude or distance."

"This is the inertia force for an ideal body moving at the assumed acceleration. An actual bridge can have different deck and ground accelerations, several vibration modes, and nonlinear behavior. This calculation is not a prediction of bridge base shear, damage, or safety."

"Investigate: match the natural frequency, predict which mode moves most, then increase damping. Does less relative motion always mean the lowest deck acceleration? Explain using the comparison and energy readings."
"Move the ground, ride the deck, and follow how motion stores and dissipates energy."
"Use the time slider or step button to inspect still frames. Animated playback is available in 3D when reduced motion is off."
"Ground motion → supports → deck motion ↔ elastic storage → damping and heat"

"A separate elastic teaching model: 16 seconds of synthetic shaking, then 8 seconds of free vibration. Motion is shown at 10× scale. The static member forces and safety factors below do not include this earthquake."
"These assumed modes do not predict this bridge’s earthquake safety, damage, or total energy. Earthquake magnitude cannot be inferred from these controls."

"The deck’s inertia resists changes in motion as its supports move. Elastic restoring forces exchange stored energy with motion; damping removes mechanical energy. After shaking stops at 16 s, vibration continues and damping controls its decay."
